source.title: The Anabasis of Alexander
source.attribution: Arrian, The Anabasis of Alexander (trans. E. J. Chinnock), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Trust the witness who had the least reason to lie
cards.body:
Arrian was a Greek writer living under the Roman Empire, about 450 years after Alexander the Great died in 323 BC. Dozens of books about Alexander already existed, and they contradicted each other. So Arrian set a rule: he relied most on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, two men who had marched with Alexander and who wrote after his death, when no one could reward or punish them for what they said. Where his sources disagree, he tells you so.

That is still a sound test for any story you hear. Ask who was actually there, and what they stood to gain or lose by telling it one way rather than another.
cards.quote: they compiled their histories after Alexander’s death, when neither compulsion was used nor reward offered them to write anything different from what really occurred.
cards.locator: Arrian’s Preface ¶1
cards.apply_it: Next time you share a striking claim, first ask: who saw this happen, and what did they gain by telling it this way?

quiz.question: Why did Arrian trust Ptolemy and Aristobulus more than other writers?
options: They were eyewitnesses who wrote when no one could pressure or reward them
They wrote the most exciting stories
quiz.explanation: Both marched with Alexander and wrote after his death, when there was nothing to gain by bending the truth.

cards.title: A clear plan can shrink a fear before it strikes
cards.body:
In 335 BC, a year after he became king of Macedon at about twenty, Alexander marched north into the Balkan mountains of what is now Bulgaria. Thracian fighters held the pass and planned to roll loaded wagons down onto his tightly packed infantry. Alexander gave a simple order: where there was room, open the ranks and let the wagons through; where there was not, lie down and lock shields overhead. The wagons rolled over the shields and Arrian says not one man died beneath them. The fight that followed cost about 1,500 Thracian lives.

Arrian notes what happened to morale: the thing the soldiers had dreaded turned out harmless, and their courage came back. A specific plan for the worst case often does the same for us.
cards.quote: Then the Macedonians regained their courage, inasmuch as the waggons, which they had excessively dreaded, had inflicted no damage upon them.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Death of Philip and Accession of Alexander.—his Wars with the. Thracians ¶3
cards.apply_it: Name the outcome you fear most this week, then write the exact steps you would take if it happened.

quiz.question: What did Alexander order his men to do as the wagons rolled down?
options: Charge up the slope at once
Open ranks or lie down with shields locked together
quiz.explanation: Some stepped aside and others locked shields so the wagons rolled over them harmlessly, and fear turned back into confidence.

cards.title: People believe the rumour they want to be true
cards.body:
In 335 BC, while Alexander was fighting far to the north, exiles slipped back into Thebes in central Greece and urged the city to revolt. Their best argument was a rumour that Alexander had been killed in Illyria. With no news to the contrary, Arrian says, each person believed whatever pleased them most. Even when his army appeared outside the walls, the leaders insisted it must be a different Alexander.

The price was terrible. The city was stormed, many were killed, and Alexander's Greek allies voted to raze Thebes and sell its surviving people into slavery. Hopeful rumours feel like facts when we want them badly. Checking them is never more important than when the news is exactly what you hoped to hear.
cards.quote: Accordingly, as is usual in such cases, not knowing the facts, each man conjectured what was most pleasing to himself.
cards.locator: Chapter VII ¶2
cards.apply_it: Think of a piece of news you accepted quickly because you liked it. What would it take to check it today?

quiz.question: What rumour helped push Thebes into revolt?
options: That Persia had sent a huge army
That Alexander had been killed in Illyria
quiz.explanation: With no news from the north, the Thebans believed the pleasing story that Alexander was dead, and the revolt ended in the city's destruction.

cards.title: Weigh advice on its merits, not on your suspicion of the adviser
cards.body:
When Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BC, the Persian commanders met to plan their defence in what is now northwest Turkey. Memnon, a Greek from Rhodes in Persian service, gave hard advice: avoid battle, burn the crops and fodder, and let hunger drive the invaders out. The Persian nobles refused. One would not let a single house in his province burn, and the others suspected Memnon only wanted to drag the war out to win honour from the king.

They fought at the river Granicus instead and lost. Whatever Memnon's motives, his plan was the one Alexander had most reason to fear. When advice is unwelcome, ask whether it is wrong, or whether you simply distrust the person giving it.
cards.quote: because they had a suspicion that Memnon was deliberately contriving to protract the war for the purpose of obtaining honour from the king.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Alexander at the Tomb of Achilles.—memnon’s Advice Rejected by the. Persian Generals ¶3
cards.apply_it: Recall advice you dismissed because of who gave it. Judge it again as if a friend had said it.

quiz.question: Why did the Persian generals reject Memnon's plan?
options: They had a better plan from Darius
They suspected his motives and would not burn their own land
quiz.explanation: They distrusted Memnon personally and refused to destroy their provinces, so a sound strategy was set aside.

cards.title: Sometimes the first move sets the tone for everything after
cards.body:
In May 334 BC Alexander reached the river Granicus in northwest Turkey and found the Persian cavalry lined up on the steep far bank. His senior general Parmenio urged him to camp and cross at dawn, warning that a first defeat would be hard to repair. Alexander agreed the arguments had force, but said it would be a disgrace if, after crossing the Hellespont so easily, this 'brook' held them up. A delay, he thought, would hand the Persians confidence.

He attacked, and won after a fierce struggle in the river. Parmenio's caution was not foolish, and Alexander's gamble could have failed. But he understood that early moments shape how both sides see the contest. A bold, early win can change what everyone believes is possible.
cards.quote: I should feel it a disgrace, if, after crossing the Hellespont so easily, this brook (for with such an appellation he made light of the Granicus) should bar our passage for a moment.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Battle of the Granicus (B.c. 334) ¶2
cards.apply_it: Pick one project you keep postponing. What small, visible first win could you get this week to set its tone?

quiz.question: What did Alexander call the Granicus to make light of it?
quiz.explanation: He called the river a 'brook' and argued that hesitating would give the Persians fresh courage.

cards.title: Remember who stood beside you when it counted
cards.body:
In the thick of the cavalry fight at the Granicus, Alexander's spear shattered. He borrowed another, struck down a Persian noble, and was hit on the helmet by a second attacker. As a third, Spithridates, raised his blade behind the king, an officer named Clitus struck first and saved Alexander's life.

Arrian records it plainly, and the moment echoes through the rest of the story. Six years later the same Clitus, drunk and angry, would remind Alexander of it in the worst possible way. For now it is a reminder that most success rests on people who acted for us at a moment we could not see coming. It is worth saying thank you while the debt is fresh.
cards.quote: And now Spithridates from behind had already raised aloft his scimitar against the king, when Clitus, son of Dropidas, anticipated his blow
cards.locator: Chapter XV. Description of the Battle of the Granicus ¶2
cards.apply_it: Name one person who quietly saved you from a mistake or setback. Thank them this week.

quiz.question: Who saved Alexander's life at the Granicus?
quiz.explanation: Clitus, son of Dropidas, struck Spithridates before his blow could land.

cards.title: Visit the wounded and let them tell their story
cards.body:
After the Granicus, Arrian reports, Alexander buried his dead with their arms and freed their parents and children from taxes. Then he went round the wounded himself. He looked at each man's injuries, asked how and doing what duty he had been hurt, and let him talk, even boast, about what he had done. He also buried the enemy commanders and the Greek mercenaries who had died fighting against him.

The detail that stands out is the listening. He did not give a speech to the wounded; he gave them a chance to be heard. When people have paid a price for shared work, attention to their own account of it can mean more than any reward.
cards.quote: for he himself visited each man, looked at their wounds, and inquired how and in the performance of what duty they had received them, allowing them both to speak and brag of their own deeds.
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. Defeat of the Persians.—loss on Both Sides ¶2
cards.apply_it: Ask someone who worked hard on a recent project to tell you how it went for them, and just listen.

quiz.question: What did Alexander do when he visited his wounded soldiers?
options: Asked how they were hurt and let them tell of their deeds
quiz.explanation: He looked at their wounds, asked how they got them, and let them speak and even boast of what they had done.

cards.title: Fight where your strengths count, not where theirs do
cards.body:
Near Miletus on the coast of western Turkey in 334 BC, Alexander's fleet of 160 ships faced about 400 Persian vessels crewed by skilled Phoenician and Cypriot sailors. Parmenio urged a sea battle, encouraged by an eagle seen on the shore. Alexander refused. His sailors were untrained, and he would not stake his soldiers' real advantage, their skill and courage on land, on an element he called unstable. He read the eagle differently: it sat on land, so he would beat the Persian fleet by taking its ports from the shore.

Soon after, short of money, he disbanded most of his fleet. Choosing your battlefield is often half the outcome. Compete where your strengths decide things.
cards.quote: he did not wish to deliver over to the foreigners on so unstable an element the advantage which the Macedonians derived from their skill and courage
cards.locator: Chapter XVIII. Alexander Marches to Miletus and Occupies the Island of Lade ¶3
cards.apply_it: Where are you competing on someone else's terms? Name one way to move the contest onto ground where you are strong.

quiz.question: How did Alexander plan to defeat the Persian fleet?
options: By capturing its harbours with his land army
By a night attack at sea
quiz.explanation: He read the eagle on the shore as a sign to master the fleet from land, by taking the ports it depended on.

cards.title: The Gordian knot: even famous stories have more than one version
cards.body:
In 333 BC Alexander reached Gordium in central Turkey, where an ancient wagon stood in the citadel. Legend said whoever untied the knot binding its yoke would rule Asia. The cord of bark had no visible ends. Some writers say Alexander, unwilling to leave it tied, slashed it with his sword. Aristobulus, who was there, says he pulled out the wooden pin through the pole and slid the yoke free.

Arrian, unusually honest, says he cannot be sure which is true. Either way, Alexander refused to accept the problem in the form it was presented. The lesson for us is double: look for the pin, not just the knot, and hold even famous stories a little loosely.
cards.quote: How Alexander performed the feat in connection with this cord, I cannot affirm with confidence.
cards.locator: Chapter III. Alexander at Gordium ¶1
cards.apply_it: Take a problem you feel stuck on and ask: what is the 'pin' here, the hidden part that would make the knot fall apart?

quiz.question: According to Aristobulus, how did Alexander undo the Gordian knot?
options: He pulled out the pin that held the yoke to the pole
He cut it with his sword
He gave up and left it
quiz.explanation: Aristobulus says he removed the wooden pin and drew the yoke free, while other writers say he cut the cord.

cards.title: Show trust in a way people can see
cards.body:
At Tarsus in southern Turkey in 333 BC, Alexander fell dangerously ill. Only his doctor Philip thought he could save him, with a strong purging drink. As Philip mixed it, a letter arrived from Parmenio warning that the doctor had been bribed by Darius to poison the king. Alexander kept the letter in his hand, took the cup, and passed Philip the letter to read while he drank. Philip was calm, not alarmed, and Alexander recovered.

Arrian notes that the act told everyone around him that Alexander trusted his friends and would not entertain suspicion of them. Trust shown openly, at a moment of real risk, builds loyalty faster than any speech.
cards.quote: But he, having read the letter, and still holding it in his hand, took the cup which contained the medicine and gave Philip the letter to read.
cards.locator: Chapter IV. Conquest of Cappadocia.—alexander’s Illness at Tarsus ¶2
cards.apply_it: Is there someone you trust but have never shown it? Find one concrete way to show it this week.

quiz.question: What did Alexander do with Parmenio's warning letter?
options: Handed it to Philip while drinking the medicine
quiz.explanation: He gave Philip the letter to read as he drank, showing open trust in his doctor.

cards.title: Name people's deeds, and go lightly on your own
cards.body:
In November 333 BC Darius III, the Persian king, slipped round behind Alexander's army near Issus, close to modern Iskenderun in southern Turkey. Before the battle Alexander gathered his officers. He reminded them of their past victories, pointed out that the narrow ground would cancel out the Persians' numbers, and told them what was at stake. Then he did something personal: he named individual men who had done brave deeds and praised them, and he spoke of his own exploits as modestly as he could.

The officers crowded round to grasp his hand. People are moved more by hearing their own names and actions honoured than by hearing their leader's. Specific praise is one of the strongest things a leader can say.
cards.quote: and if any man had individually performed any distinguished feat of valour from love of glory, he mentioned him by name in commendation of the deed.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Darius at Issus.—alexander’s Speech to His Army ¶1
cards.apply_it: In your next team update, name one person and the specific thing they did well.

quiz.question: How did Alexander speak about his own deeds before Issus?
options: He did not mention them at all
He had others list them for him
quiz.explanation: He praised others by name and recounted his own daring as modestly as he could.

cards.title: When the leader runs, everyone runs
cards.body:
At Issus, Alexander's charge broke the Persian left. Darius saw that part of his army cut off and, Arrian says, fled at once in his chariot, then abandoned it with his shield, cloak and bow and escaped on horseback as night fell. The rest of the Persian army collapsed in panic, many trampled in the narrow roads. Arrian reports around 100,000 Persian dead, a figure modern historians treat with great caution, but the slaughter was clearly huge. Darius's mother, wife and children were captured in his camp.

A leader's behaviour under pressure travels instantly through the ranks. Calm spreads, and so does fear. In a crisis, the people who look to you take their cue from what you do, not what you say.
cards.quote: But as soon as the left wing of Darius was terrified and routed by Alexander, and the Persian king perceived that this part of his army was severed from the rest, without any further delay he began to flee in his chariot
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Defeat and Flight of Darius ¶2
cards.apply_it: When things go wrong at work or home this week, notice what your face and voice are signalling to those around you.

quiz.question: What did Darius leave behind in his chariot as he fled Issus?
quiz.explanation: He abandoned his shield, Median mantle and bow in the chariot and fled on horseback; Alexander captured them.

cards.title: Spare people's embarrassment when they get it wrong
cards.body:
After Issus the captured family of Darius believed he was dead, because Alexander had his chariot and weapons. Alexander sent word that Darius was alive and that the women would keep their royal rank and title. One story, which Arrian repeats while admitting he cannot be sure of it, goes further. When Alexander visited the tent with his closest friend Hephaestion, Darius's mother bowed to Hephaestion, the taller man. Told her mistake, she was mortified. Alexander said she had made no mistake, for Hephaestion was also an Alexander.

Arrian praises the kindness whether or not it happened. One gracious sentence turned a humiliating slip into an honour for everyone present. Rescuing someone from embarrassment costs little and is remembered for life.
cards.quote: But the king told her she had made no mistake, for Hephaestion was also an Alexander.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Kind Treatment of Darius’s Family ¶2
cards.apply_it: Next time someone makes an awkward mistake in front of you, look for a kind word that lets them save face.

quiz.question: What did Alexander say when Darius's mother bowed to Hephaestion by mistake?
options: That Hephaestion was also an Alexander
quiz.explanation: He told her she had not erred, because Hephaestion was 'also an Alexander', turning her mistake into an honour.

cards.title: 'If I were Parmenio': ambition sets the size of the deal you'll take
cards.body:
While Alexander was besieging Tyre in 332 BC, envoys arrived from Darius with a generous offer: 10,000 talents for his family, all the land west of the Euphrates, and his daughter in marriage. Parmenio said that if he were Alexander, he would gladly accept and end the war without more risk. Alexander is said to have replied that so would he, if he were Parmenio. But he was Alexander, and he turned it down.

The exchange shows how two sensible people can read the same offer completely differently, depending on what they want from life. It also shows the danger: the same refusal to settle led Alexander's men on for years more of war. Know which of the two you are being, and why.
cards.quote: Alexander is said to have replied, So would he also do, if he were Parmenio, but as he was Alexander he replied to Darius as he did.
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. The Offers of Darius Rejected.—batis, Governor of Gaza, Refuses to. Submit ¶1
cards.apply_it: Facing a choice between a good deal now and a bigger gamble, write down what you truly want before you decide.

quiz.question: What did Darius offer Alexander during the siege of Tyre?
options: Money, all land west of the Euphrates and his daughter in marriage
quiz.explanation: Darius offered 10,000 talents, the land west of the Euphrates and marriage to his daughter. Parmenio would have accepted.

cards.title: Secure your base before you chase the big prize
cards.body:
After Issus it was tempting to chase Darius straight into Mesopotamia. Instead, in 332 BC, Alexander turned to Tyre, an island city off the coast of what is now Lebanon, after it refused to let him in. He explained his reasoning to his officers: while Persia ruled the sea, Tyre, Egypt and Cyprus could be used to carry the war back into Greece behind him. Take Tyre, and the Phoenician fleet would likely come over; then Cyprus and Egypt would follow, and he could march on Babylon with home secure.

It was a long and bloody detour, and it worked as he predicted. Before chasing your biggest goal, ask what could undo you from behind.
cards.quote: nor is it a safe course, both for other reasons, and especially looking at the state of matters in Greece, for us to pursue Darius, leaving in our rear the city of Tyre itself in doubtful allegiance, and Egypt and Cyprus in the occupation of the Persians.
cards.locator: Chapter XVII. Speech of Alexander to His Officers ¶1
cards.apply_it: Before your next big push, list one weak spot behind you that could undo the gains. Fix it first.

quiz.question: Why did Alexander decide to take Tyre before pursuing Darius?
options: He needed its gold to pay his army
Leaving it hostile behind him risked the war spreading back to Greece
quiz.explanation: While Persia held the sea, an unconquered Tyre, Egypt and Cyprus behind him could threaten Greece.

cards.title: Lead the hard work from the front
cards.body:
Tyre stood on an island with high walls, and Persia still ruled the sea. Alexander's answer was to build a causeway, called a mole, of stones and timber out across the strait to the city. Arrian says the Macedonians worked with real zeal, and that it grew because Alexander himself was there leading everything, encouraging the men with words and rewarding those who toiled hardest. As the mole reached deeper water, the builders came under fire from the walls and from Tyrian ships, so towers and screens had to be raised to protect them.

People work harder for a leader who is visibly in it with them. Your presence at the hardest part of a job says more than any memo.
cards.quote: The zeal of the Macedonians in the work was great, and it was increased by the presence of Alexander himself, who took the lead
cards.locator: Chapter XVIII. Siege of Tyre.—construction of a Mole From the Mainland to the Island ¶1
cards.apply_it: Find the least glamorous part of a current team task and spend an hour doing it alongside the others.

quiz.question: How did Alexander try to reach the island city of Tyre?
options: By starving it for ten years
By building a mole of stones and timber out to it
By landing at night in small boats
quiz.explanation: He built a causeway across the strait, and his personal presence spurred the men on.

cards.title: Long frustration can turn into cruelty if no one checks it
cards.body:
Tyre fell in the summer of 332 BC after a long siege by land and sea. Arrian is frank about the end. The Macedonians stormed in full of rage, angry at the length of the siege and because the Tyrians had killed captured Macedonians on the walls in full view of the camp. Arrian reports about 8,000 Tyrians killed and about 30,000 people sold into slavery. Alexander spared those who took refuge in the temple of Heracles, including the king of Tyre.

Behind the strategy lay terrible human suffering. Frustration that builds over a long struggle can explode once resistance breaks. When you finally win a hard fight, watch your anger at the moment it is safe to let it out.
cards.quote: For the Macedonians were now for the most part advancing full of rage, being angry both at the length of the siege
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Capture of Tyre ¶1
cards.apply_it: After a long conflict ends in your favour, pause before your next move and ask whether anger is driving it.

quiz.question: According to Arrian, why were the Macedonians so enraged when they stormed Tyre?
options: The siege had been long and the Tyrians had killed Macedonian captives
quiz.explanation: Anger at the long siege and the killing of captives on the walls fed the slaughter.

cards.title: See the potential in a place before others do
cards.body:
In 332 BC the Persian governor of Egypt, with no army left to resist, let Alexander in without a fight. Early in 331 BC, sailing along the coast west of the Nile delta, Alexander saw a stretch of shore between the sea and a lake and was taken with the idea of founding a city there. He marked out the boundaries himself: where the marketplace would be, which temples to build, including one to the Egyptian goddess Isis, and where the wall would run.

That city was Alexandria, which became one of the great centres of learning and trade in the ancient world and is still Egypt's second city. Good founders look past what a place is to what it could become.
cards.quote: The position seemed to him a very fine one in which to found a city, and he foresaw that it would become a prosperous one.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Conquest of Egypt.—foundation of Alexandria ¶1
cards.apply_it: Look at something ordinary you work with every day. What could it become with a clear plan behind it?

quiz.question: Which temple did Alexander mark out in Alexandria alongside the Greek ones?
quiz.explanation: He marked a spot for a temple to the Egyptian Isis, a sign the city was meant to belong to Egypt too.

cards.title: Be honest about why you are really making the journey
cards.body:
In 331 BC Alexander crossed the desert to the oracle of the god Ammon at the Siwa oasis in western Egypt. Arrian says he went partly to rival the heroes Perseus and Heracles, who were said to have consulted it, and partly to learn more surely about his own origins, since he traced his descent from Ammon, or at least to be able to say he had. The guides lost the way in shifting sand; Ptolemy said two serpents led them, Aristobulus said two ravens. Alexander, Arrian says, heard the answer he wanted.

Arrian's phrase 'or at least that he might be able to say' is sharp. Sometimes we chase not the truth, but a story we can tell about ourselves.
cards.quote: Accordingly he made the expedition to Ammon with the design of learning his own origin more certainly, or at least that he might be able to say that he had learned it.
cards.locator: Chapter III. Alexander Visits the Temple of Ammon ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you are pursuing. Are you after the thing itself, or the story you'll be able to tell about it?

quiz.question: According to Ptolemy, what guided Alexander's army through the desert to Siwa?
quiz.explanation: Ptolemy said two serpents led the way; Aristobulus said two ravens. Arrian notes the accounts disagree.

cards.title: Let each leader rally their own people
cards.body:
In 331 BC Darius gathered a vast army on the plain of Gaugamela, near modern Mosul in northern Iraq. Alexander first took Parmenio's advice to stop and scout the ground. Then, instead of a grand speech to the whole army, he told his officers that the men did not need his words to be brave. Each captain should rouse his own company, each cavalry leader his own squadron. He asked only for discipline: silence when silence helped, a great shout when shouting helped, and orders passed down fast.

Messages land best from the person people work with every day. A short, clear brief to your leaders, who then speak to their own teams in their own words, often beats one big address.
cards.quote: He thought it expedient that each of them individually should stir up his own men separately; the infantry captain the men of his company, the cavalry captain his own squadron, the brigadiers their various brigades
cards.locator: Chapter IX. Alexander’s Tactics.—his Speech to the Officers ¶1
cards.apply_it: Before your next big change, brief your team leads and let each explain it to their own people.

quiz.question: How did Alexander want his troops encouraged before Gaugamela?
options: By one long speech from himself
By each officer rousing his own unit
quiz.explanation: He asked each captain and leader to stir up his own men and stressed discipline and quick orders.

cards.title: Win in daylight, so no one can say you stole it
cards.body:
On the night before Gaugamela, Parmenio came to Alexander's tent and urged a surprise night attack on the huge Persian army. With others listening, Alexander answered that it would be mean to steal a victory; he should win openly and without tricks.

Arrian admires this, but also shows the cool thinking behind it. Night battles are chaotic and can hand victory to the weaker side; the ground was unfamiliar and full of enemies; and if Darius lost by day he could not blame the dark. A clean win is harder to dispute. On 1 October 331 BC the battle was fought in daylight, and Darius fled again. Sometimes the honourable path and the wise path turn out to be the same one.
cards.quote: But the reply which he made, as others were listening to their conversation, was, that it would be mean to steal a victory, and that Alexander ought to conquer in open daylight, and without any artifice.
cards.locator: Chapter X. Rejection of Parmenio’s Advice ¶1
cards.apply_it: Is there a shortcut tempting you that would make your success easy to question? Consider the open route instead.

quiz.question: Besides honour, what practical reason does Arrian give for refusing a night attack?
options: Night battles are unpredictable and can hand victory to the weaker side
quiz.explanation: Arrian notes that in the dark many accidents happen, and a defeated Darius could have blamed the night.

cards.title: Revenge for old wrongs can damage what you now own
cards.body:
Early in 330 BC Alexander took Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Persian kings in southern Iran. He burned the royal palace. Parmenio argued against it: it was now Alexander's own property, and the people of Asia would conclude he meant only to conquer and leave, not to rule them. Alexander said he was taking vengeance for the Persian invasion of Greece a century and a half earlier, when Athens and its temples were burned.

Arrian, usually his admirer, says flatly that Alexander was not acting wisely, and that this punished no one who had actually done the harm. Settling old scores often hurts the present far more than the past. Ask who the punishment really reaches.
cards.quote: But Alexander does not seem to me to have acted on this occasion with prudence; nor do I think that this was any retributive penalty at all on the ancient Persians.
cards.locator: Chapter XVIII. Defeat of Ariobarzanes and Capture of Persepolis ¶2
cards.apply_it: Think of a grudge you're tempted to act on. Who would the consequences actually fall on today?

quiz.question: Why did Parmenio advise against burning the palace at Persepolis?
options: It was now Alexander's property, and Asians would think he did not mean to stay
The army needed it for winter quarters
quiz.explanation: He warned that destroying his own property would signal to Asia that Alexander only meant to conquer and depart.

cards.title: Honour a fallen rival, even when you beat them
cards.body:
After Gaugamela, Darius fled east. In July 330 BC, in what is now northern Iran, his own nobles led by Bessus arrested him and carried him in chains. As Alexander closed in after a desperate chase, they stabbed the king and left him; he died before Alexander reached him, at about fifty. Arrian lists the run of disasters in his short reign, ending in betrayal by those closest to him.

Alexander sent Darius's body to be buried in the royal tombs like the kings before him, and raised his children as royalty. Respect for a defeated opponent costs the winner nothing and says a great deal about them. It also made Alexander look like a rightful successor, not just a conqueror.
cards.quote: but after his death he received a royal burial; his children received from Alexander a princely rearing and education, just as if their father had still been king
cards.locator: Chapter XXII. Reflections on the Fate of Darius ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of a rival who has had a setback. What small act of respect could you show them?

quiz.question: Who killed Darius III?
options: His own nobles, led by Bessus and his allies
quiz.explanation: Bessus and fellow nobles arrested him and, with Alexander close behind, wounded him and left him to die.

cards.title: Fear of what someone might do can destroy the innocent too
cards.body:
In 330 BC, in what is now western Afghanistan, Alexander learned of a plot against his life. Philotas, son of Parmenio and commander of the elite cavalry, had heard of it and said nothing, though he visited the king twice a day. Tried before the Macedonians, he and others were executed. Then Alexander sent secret orders to have Parmenio, his oldest general, killed in Media. Arrian suggests why: either Alexander could not believe the father was innocent, or he feared Parmenio would be dangerous after his son's death, being so respected by the army.

Arrian does not claim Parmenio was guilty. Acting on fear of what a person might do, rather than what they have done, is how good people get destroyed.
cards.quote: or perhaps, he thought that even if he had no share in it, he would now be a dangerous man if he survived, after the king had violently made away with his son.
cards.locator: Chapter XXVI. Philotas and Parmenio Put to Death ¶1
cards.apply_it: Are you judging someone by what they've done, or by what you fear they might do? Check the evidence.

quiz.question: What was Philotas convicted of?
options: Knowing of a plot against Alexander and not reporting it
quiz.explanation: He admitted hearing of a conspiracy but had said nothing, though he saw the king twice daily.

cards.title: No achievement brings happiness without self-control
cards.body:
In 329 BC, at Bactra in what is now northern Afghanistan, Bessus, the man who had betrayed Darius, was brought before Alexander. Alexander ordered his nose and ears cut off before he was sent to be executed. Arrian refuses to praise it. He calls the mutilation barbaric, and criticises Alexander for adopting Persian royal dress and treating his subjects as inferiors.

Then Arrian makes one of the central points of his whole book. Imagine a man stronger, better born and more successful than Alexander, who conquered Asia, Africa and Europe. None of it would add to his happiness unless he could also govern himself. Power, fame and success magnify whatever is inside a person, including their lack of restraint.
cards.quote: all these things would be no furtherance to such a man’s happiness, unless at the same time he possess the power of self-control, though he has performed the great deeds which have been supposed.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Treatment of Bessus ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick one area where success has made you less careful. Set one clear limit for yourself there.

quiz.question: What does Arrian say is needed for great achievements to bring happiness?
quiz.explanation: Arrian argues that conquering the world adds nothing to happiness without the power of self-control.

cards.title: Flatterers set the fire, but drink and anger light it
cards.body:
In Central Asia around 328 BC, at a long drinking party, courtiers flattered Alexander by ranking him above the gods' sons Castor and Pollux, and even belittled his father Philip. Clitus, the man who had saved his life at the Granicus, had long resented Alexander's new Persian style and the flatterers around him. Drunk, he hit back, praised Philip, mocked Alexander, and finally held up his hand: 'This hand saved you.' Friends dragged him out, but he came back. Alexander, enraged and drunk, seized a spear and killed him.

Arrian blames Clitus for his insolence, but saves his sharpest words for the flatterers who corrupt kings. Rooms full of praise and wine make terrible decisions.
cards.quote: Such men have always corrupted the character of kings and will never cease to ruin the interests of those who happen to be reigning.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. The Murder of Clitus ¶1
cards.apply_it: Notice who around you only ever agrees with you. Seek out one honest voice this week.

quiz.question: Whom does Arrian blame most sharply for corrupting kings?
quiz.explanation: He says flatterers have always corrupted kings, though he also criticises Clitus and Alexander's anger and drinking.

cards.title: Own the wrong you did instead of defending it
cards.body:
After killing Clitus, Alexander saw at once what he had done. Some writers say he tried to fall on the spear himself. Most say he lay in bed lamenting, calling out Clitus's name and that of Clitus's sister, who had been his own nurse, and calling himself the murderer of his friends. For three days he refused food and drink.

Arrian pities him as a slave, that night, to anger and drunkenness. But he praises what came after: Alexander did not dig in or justify the wrong, but admitted he had done it, being a man and not a god. When a philosopher later told him whatever a king does is just, Arrian calls that advice more harmful than the crime itself.
cards.quote: I think Alexander deserves great praise for this, that he did not obstinately persevere in evil, or still worse become a defender and advocate of the wrong which had been done
cards.locator: Chapter IX. Alexander’s Grief for Clitus ¶1
cards.apply_it: Is there a wrong you've been quietly justifying? Write one honest sentence admitting it.

quiz.question: What does Arrian praise in Alexander's behaviour after the death of Clitus?
options: That he admitted the crime instead of defending it
That he blamed the god Dionysus
quiz.explanation: Arrian praises him for confessing the wrong rather than becoming its advocate.

cards.title: Speak the truth to power, but mind how you say it
cards.body:
In 327 BC at Bactra, Alexander's court tried to introduce prostration, the Persian custom of bowing to the ground before the king, for Greeks and Macedonians too. The historian Callisthenes objected in front of everyone. Alexander deserved every honour fit for a human being, he said, but not honours meant for gods; free Greeks would never bow like this. The Macedonians quietly agreed, and Alexander dropped the plan for them.

Arrian's verdict is mixed. Callisthenes was right in substance, but blunt and tactless; he could have made his point discreetly. Alexander came to hate him; he was later accused over a plot and died a prisoner, though the sources disagree how. Honest dissent matters, but how and when you say it decides whether it is heard.
cards.quote: I openly declare that there is no honour which Alexander is unworthy to receive, provided that it is consistent with his being human
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Callisthenes Opposes the Proposal to Honour Alexander by Prostration ¶1
cards.apply_it: Before you disagree with someone senior, plan how to say it so they can accept it without losing face.

quiz.question: What custom did Callisthenes oppose?
quiz.explanation: He argued prostration belonged to gods, not men. Arrian thought he was right but tactless in how he said it.

cards.title: Decency is noticed, even by your enemies
cards.body:
In 327 BC, on a mountain stronghold called the Sogdian Rock in what is now Uzbekistan or Tajikistan, Alexander captured the family of a local noble, Oxyartes. Arrian says Alexander fell in love with the daughter, Roxana, but would not force himself on a captive and instead married her. Years earlier, he had also treated Darius's captive wife with respect.

Arrian tells a story about that: when Darius heard his wife had been treated honourably, he prayed that if he must lose his empire, it should go to no one but Alexander. Arrian concludes that even enemies care about decent conduct. Oxyartes, hearing his daughter was respected, came over to Alexander. How you treat people with no power over you shapes your reputation more than anything.
cards.quote: Thus not even to enemies, I ween, are chaste actions a matter of unconcern.
cards.locator: Chapter XX. Magnanimous Treatment of the Family of Darius ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who depends on you and cannot push back. How would they describe the way you treat them?

quiz.question: What did Darius pray after hearing how his wife had been treated?
options: That if he lost his empire, it should go to Alexander
quiz.explanation: Moved by Alexander's respect for his family, Darius asked that his power pass to no one but Alexander.

cards.title: Repeat a false alarm until your opponent stops reacting
cards.body:
In spring 326 BC Alexander reached the river Hydaspes, now the Jhelum in Pakistan's Punjab. On the far bank waited King Porus with a strong army and many war elephants, which would terrify the Macedonian horses. The river was swollen with monsoon rain and snowmelt. Alexander let it be known he might wait for winter. Meanwhile, night after night, his cavalry made noise along the bank as if about to cross. Porus marched his elephants to meet each alarm until, finding them empty, he stopped.

Then Alexander crossed for real at a wooded bend upstream, out of sight. It is a lesson worth knowing from both sides: repeated false alarms train us to ignore the real one.
cards.quote: When Alexander had brought it about that the mind of Porus no longer entertained any fear of his nocturnal attempts, he devised the following stratagem.
cards.locator: Chapter X. Alexander and Porus at the Hydaspes ¶1
cards.apply_it: Is there a warning you've learned to ignore because it's gone off before? Check it properly once more.

quiz.question: Why did Porus eventually stop responding to the night-time noise?
options: Repeated alarms came to nothing, so he judged them harmless
quiz.explanation: After many empty alarms he decided his fear had been groundless and stayed in camp, so the real crossing surprised him.

cards.title: 'Treat me as a king': dignity in defeat can win respect
cards.body:
At the Hydaspes, Porus fought on long after his army was breaking, not fleeing as Darius had done. Arrian reports about 20,000 Indian infantry and 3,000 cavalry killed, among them two of Porus's sons. Wounded, Porus finally withdrew, and Alexander, admiring his courage, sent messengers to bring him in. When they met, Alexander asked how he wished to be treated. Porus answered: 'Treat me, O Alexander, in a kingly way.' Asked if he wanted anything more, he said that covered everything.

Alexander gave him back his kingdom and added more land, and Porus stayed loyal from then on. Carrying yourself with dignity in defeat earns more than pleading, and honouring a worthy opponent can turn them into an ally.
cards.quote: Treat me, O Alexander, in a kingly way!
cards.locator: Chapter XIX. Alliance with Porus.—death of Bucephalas ¶1
cards.apply_it: After your next setback, decide how you want to carry yourself and say it plainly.

quiz.question: What did Alexander give Porus after his defeat?
options: A post as a cavalry officer
His own kingdom back, plus more land
quiz.explanation: Pleased by his answer, Alexander restored Porus's rule and enlarged it, and Porus stayed faithful.

cards.title: Persuade by sharing the burden, not just the vision
cards.body:
In 326 BC Alexander's army reached the river Hyphasis, the Beas in northern India, after eight years on the march. Alexander wanted to push on to the Ganges and the Ocean he believed circled the earth. His soldiers had had enough. He called his officers together and said he would either persuade them or be persuaded. He listed their conquests and, above all, insisted he was no general sitting safe while others bled: the labour and danger were shared, the rewards open to all.

It was a strong speech, and it is a fair test of any leader's ask: are you sharing the costs you are asking others to bear? Here, though, persuasion met its limit.
cards.quote: But now the labours are common to you and me, we have an equal share of the dangers, and the rewards are open to the free competition of all.
cards.locator: Chapter XXVI ¶2
cards.apply_it: When you next ask your team for extra effort, say specifically what you will take on yourself.

quiz.question: What did Alexander say at the start of his speech at the Hyphasis?
options: That he would punish anyone who refused
That the gods demanded they continue
That he would either persuade them or be persuaded by them
That the war was nearly over
quiz.explanation: He opened by offering to persuade them or be persuaded, then argued that labours and dangers were shared.

cards.title: Someone has to break the silence, and say it with respect
cards.body:
After Alexander's speech at the Hyphasis, there was a long silence. No one dared contradict the king, and no one wanted to agree. He kept inviting anyone with a different view to speak. At last Coenus, a veteran commander, spoke for the ordinary soldiers. He reminded Alexander how few of the original army remained, how many had died of disease or wounds, and how much the men longed for their parents, wives and children. Go home, he said, and come back with fresh troops if you wish.

He ended with a line that sums up the book: self-control in the midst of success is the noblest virtue. The officers applauded and many wept. Honest words, said with respect, can speak for many.
cards.quote: Self-control in the midst of success is the noblest of all virtues, O king!
cards.locator: Chapter XXVII. The Answer of Coenus ¶1
cards.apply_it: In your next meeting where everyone is silent, be the one who respectfully says what others are thinking.

quiz.question: Whose interests did Coenus say he was speaking for?
options: His own and the senior officers'
quiz.explanation: Coenus said he was speaking not for himself but for the bulk of the army, who were exhausted and longed for home.

cards.title: Sulking rarely changes minds; listening does
cards.body:
Annoyed by Coenus's frankness, Alexander broke up the meeting. The next day he said angrily that he would go on with whoever chose to follow, and the rest could go home and tell their families they had abandoned their king among enemies. Then he shut himself in his tent for three days, waiting for the mood to shift, as it often did among soldiers. It did not. The camp stayed silent and resentful.

At last, after the sacrifices for crossing proved unfavourable, he called his oldest friends and announced the army would turn back. Turning back from the Hyphasis was the end of his eastward march. Withdrawing to make people feel your displeasure seldom works. Hearing them does.
cards.quote: he retired into his tent, and did not admit any of the Companions on that day, or until the third day from that, waiting to see if any change would occur in the minds of the Macedonians
cards.locator: Chapter XXVIII. Alexander Resolves to Return ¶1
cards.apply_it: When you feel like withdrawing to make a point, ask one person directly what they need instead.

quiz.question: What happened while Alexander stayed in his tent for three days?
options: The army changed its mind and agreed to advance
The officers elected a new leader
The army marched home without him
The camp remained silent and unchanged
quiz.explanation: The soldiers were annoyed at his anger but not moved by it, and he finally agreed to turn back.

cards.title: The criticism that stings most is often the one that's true
cards.body:
Around 325 BC, attacking a town of the Mallians near modern Multan in Pakistan, Alexander climbed a ladder ahead of his men, then leapt alone into the citadel. The ladders behind him broke. He was shot through the chest and nearly died, saved by a few men who covered him with shields. Arrian records that his enraged soldiers then killed everyone in the town, sparing not even women or children.

When he recovered, friends rebuked him: fighting in the front line was a soldier's job, not a general's. He was offended. Arrian's explanation is acute: Alexander was angry because he knew they were right. When criticism stings, it is worth asking whether it stings because it is true.
cards.quote: It seems to me that Alexander was offended at these remarks, because he knew that they were correct, and that he deserved the censure.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Joy of the Soldiers at Alexander’s Recovery ¶1
cards.apply_it: Recall a recent criticism that annoyed you. Write down the part of it that might be true.

quiz.question: Why, according to Arrian, was Alexander offended by his friends' rebuke?
options: He knew they were right and deserved it
They had not been in the battle
quiz.explanation: Arrian thinks he was offended precisely because the criticism was correct.

cards.title: In a crisis, let people see you, not just hear about you
cards.body:
While Alexander lay wounded, news reached the main camp that he was dead. The army fell into grief and fear: who would lead them, and how would they get home through hostile lands? Even a letter from the king did not convince them; they assumed his officers had forged it. So, as soon as he could travel, Alexander had himself carried by boat to the camp, with the awning removed so everyone could see him. He raised his hand to the crowd, called for his horse rather than a stretcher, and walked the last stretch to his tent.

Rumour beats written reassurance. When people are frightened, they need to see you with their own eyes.
cards.quote: When the ship bearing the king approached the camp, he ordered the tent covering to be removed from the stern, that he might be visible to all.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Joy of the Soldiers at Alexander’s Recovery ¶1
cards.apply_it: If your team is anxious about a change, show up in person this week rather than sending another email.

quiz.question: Why didn't Alexander's letter calm the army?
options: They thought it had been forged by his officers
quiz.explanation: Fearing the worst, the soldiers assumed his bodyguards and generals had written it, so only seeing him convinced them.

cards.title: Wanting to outdo legends can cost other people dearly
cards.body:
In 325 BC, coming back from India, Alexander led part of his army west through the Gedrosian desert, the Makran coast of southern Pakistan and Iran. His admiral Nearchus said Alexander knew how hard it was, but had heard that only the legendary queen Semiramis and the Persian founder Cyrus had brought armies through, each losing almost everything, and he wanted to outdo them. He also hoped to supply his fleet along the coast.

Arrian describes sixty days of heat, deep sand, thirst and flash flood. Many soldiers, and many of the women and children with the army, died. Ambition to do what no one has done can be inspiring, but count who pays the price when the leader's dream is tested.
cards.quote: When Alexander received this information he was seized with a desire of excelling Cyrus and Semiramis.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. March Through Gadrosia ¶1
cards.apply_it: Before your next big personal challenge, list who else would carry the cost if it goes wrong.

quiz.question: Whom did Alexander want to outdo by crossing the Gedrosian desert?
quiz.explanation: Nearchus says he wanted to excel Cyrus and Semiramis, who had barely escaped the desert with a handful of men.

cards.title: Know when it's wiser not to notice
cards.body:
In the Gedrosian desert, food ran short. The soldiers began secretly killing the pack horses and mules for meat, then claiming the animals had died of thirst or heat. Everyone was involved, so no one told. Arrian says Alexander knew perfectly well, but judged that pretending not to know was a better cure than either punishing desperate men or openly approving it.

There was a heavy cost: without pack animals, the sick and exhausted could not be carried, and many were left behind in the sand. Arrian also notes that Alexander camped some distance from water, so thirsty men would not rush in and drown or foul it. Leading in a crisis means choosing which rules to enforce, and accepting what that choice costs.
cards.quote: he saw that the best cure for the present state of affairs would be to pretend to be ignorant of it, rather than to permit it as a thing known to himself.
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Sufferings of the Army ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of a minor rule being bent under pressure around you. Would enforcing it now help, or just add strain?

quiz.question: How did Alexander handle the soldiers secretly killing pack animals for food?
quiz.explanation: He judged that ignoring it was the best remedy, neither punishing nor openly allowing it.

cards.title: Refuse a comfort your people cannot share
cards.body:
Leading his army on foot through scorching sand, thirsty like everyone else, Alexander was brought a helmet of water that a few light troops had scraped from a muddy pool. He thanked them, then poured it on the ground in front of the whole army. Arrian says the effect was as if every man had drunk.

Arrian calls this perhaps the noblest thing Alexander ever did, proof of his endurance and self-control and of his skill in leading men. Soon after, when the guides lost the way, he rode ahead with a handful of men, found the sea and dug for fresh water on the beach. Sharing hardship openly can lift people more than any reward. Small privileges a leader quietly refuses are often noticed most.
cards.quote: He took it, and commending the men who brought it, immediately poured it upon the ground in the sight of all.
cards.locator: Chapter XXVI. Alexander’s Magnanimous Conduct ¶1
cards.apply_it: Look for one small perk you enjoy that your team does not. Consider giving it up or sharing it.

quiz.question: What effect did Arrian say pouring out the water had on the army?
options: It made them doubt his sanity
It refreshed them as if every man had drunk
quiz.explanation: Arrian says the army was reinvigorated as though the water had given each man a drink.

cards.title: Even the greatest founders ask only for a quiet grave
cards.body:
In 324 BC, back in Persia, Alexander visited the tomb of Cyrus the Great at Pasargadae in southern Iran. Cyrus had founded the Persian Empire two centuries earlier. Alexander found the tomb broken into and robbed, the body thrown out. He was grieved, and ordered Aristobulus to restore it, put back the remains, and seal the door. He had the guards questioned under torture; they confessed nothing and were released.

The inscription on the tomb, as Arrian records it, named Cyrus as founder of the Persian Empire and king of Asia, and asked only one thing of passers-by: not to begrudge him his small monument. Every empire passes. Respect for those who came before is something we choose.
cards.quote: O man, I am Cyrus, son of Cambyses, who founded the empire of the Persians, and was king of Asia. Do not therefore grudge me this monument.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIX. Alexander in Persis.—tomb of Cyrus Repaired ¶2
cards.apply_it: Name someone who built what you now benefit from. Find a way to honour their work this month.

quiz.question: What did Alexander find when he visited the tomb of Cyrus?
options: It had been turned into a temple
It had been broken into and robbed
It had been moved to Babylon
quiz.explanation: The tomb had been dug through and pillaged; Alexander ordered it restored and sealed.

cards.title: Admiring wise words is not the same as living by them
cards.body:
Arrian tells how some Indian sages, seeing Alexander and his army, simply stamped on the ground. Asked why, they said every man owns only as much earth as he stands on; Alexander was only a man, troubling himself and others across the world, and would soon own just enough to be buried in. At Taxila, in what is now Pakistan, the elder sage Dandamis refused to join him, saying he wanted nothing. Earlier, the Greek philosopher Diogenes had asked him only to stand out of his sunlight.

Alexander admired them all. But, Arrian says, he did the opposite of what he praised, being a slave to insatiable ambition. Nodding at wisdom is easy; changing course because of it is the hard part.
cards.quote: On this occasion Alexander commended both the words and the men who spoke them; but nevertheless he did just the opposite to that which he commended.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Alexander’s Dealings with the Indian Sages ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick a piece of advice you often agree with but don't follow. Take one step on it today.

quiz.question: What did the Indian sages mean by stamping on the ground?
options: Each man truly owns only the earth he stands on, and soon his grave
They were angry at the army
They wanted Alexander to leave their meadow
quiz.explanation: They said a man possesses only as much earth as he stands on, and Alexander too would soon need only a grave.

cards.title: When people distrust your offer, remove the reason to fear it
cards.body:
In 324 BC at Susa, in southwest Iran, Alexander offered to pay off all his soldiers' debts and asked them to register what they owed. Few did. They feared it was a test to find out who was overspending. Alexander scolded them for distrusting him, then changed the method: tables of money were set up in camp, and anyone showing a debt bond was paid, with no names recorded. The total, reportedly, was 20,000 talents.

Arrian says the men valued the anonymity even more than being free of debt. Good intentions are not enough when people fear how information will be used. Make the help easy to accept without exposing anyone.
cards.quote: the fact that they were not known was a greater pleasure to them than the fact that they ceased to be in debt.
cards.locator: Chapter V. The Soldiers Rewarded ¶1
cards.apply_it: If people are slow to take up help you offer, ask what they fear it might reveal, and remove that risk.

quiz.question: Why did few soldiers at first register their debts?
options: They did not trust the treasurer's maths
They feared it was a test of who was extravagant
quiz.explanation: They suspected Alexander wanted to find out who was overspending, so he paid debts anonymously instead.

cards.title: 'Show me your wounds and I'll show you mine'
cards.body:
In 324 BC at Opis, on the Tigris near modern Baghdad, Alexander announced he would send home veterans who were too old or injured to fight. The Macedonians, already resentful of his Persian dress and the foreign troops trained in their style, took it as an insult and shouted that he should dismiss them all. In fury he had thirteen ringleaders seized for execution, then gave one of the most famous speeches in history.

He reminded them what Philip had made of them and what he had won for them, saying he kept nothing but his purple robe and crown. Then: let anyone with wounds show them, and he would show his. A leader's credibility rests on visible shared cost.
cards.quote: Come now! whoever of you has wounds, let him strip and show them, and I will show mine in turn
cards.locator: Chapter X ¶2
cards.apply_it: Before asking for loyalty, list what you have personally given up for the shared goal. Is it visible to others?

quiz.question: What sparked the protest at Opis?
options: Alexander's plan to send home old and injured veterans
quiz.explanation: The soldiers felt despised when he announced the discharge of the unfit, and demanded he dismiss them all.

cards.title: A single word of belonging can end a quarrel
cards.body:
After the speech at Opis, Alexander shut himself away for two days. On the third he began giving commands to Persians and calling them his kinsmen. The Macedonians broke. They ran to the palace, threw down their weapons, and begged to be let in. Alexander came out and wept. A veteran officer, Callines, told him what hurt: Persians were called his kinsmen and could greet him with a kiss, and no Macedonian could. Alexander replied that he counted every one of them his kin.

They kissed him and went back singing. At a banquet he prayed for harmony between Macedonians and Persians. Beneath many conflicts lies a simple fear of not belonging. Naming people as your own can heal it.
cards.quote: But all of you without exception I consider my kinsmen, and so from this time I shall call you.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Reconciliation Between Alexander and His Army ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who feels left out. Tell them clearly that they belong.

quiz.question: What did Callines say was really hurting the Macedonians?
options: That Persians, not Macedonians, were called the king's kinsmen
quiz.explanation: Callines said it grieved them that Persians were honoured as kinsmen while no Macedonian was, and Alexander declared them all his kin.

cards.title: Great grief is the shadow of great love
cards.body:
In autumn 324 BC, at Ecbatana (modern Hamadan in Iran), Hephaestion, Alexander's closest friend since boyhood, fell ill with fever and died before Alexander reached him. Arrian notes that writers told wildly different stories about what Alexander then did, some to flatter and some to blame him. But all agreed his grief was immense. For three days he neither ate nor cared for his appearance, but lay on the ground mourning. He kept Hephaestion's name on his cavalry unit so it would not be forgotten.

Arrian records Alexander saying he had valued Hephaestion as much as his own life. Grief this deep is not weakness; it reflects how much someone mattered. Honouring a person's memory can be part of carrying on.
cards.quote: they agree in this, that his grief was great.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. Death of Hephaestion ¶1
cards.apply_it: If you are grieving someone, find one small way to keep their name present, like Alexander did.

quiz.question: How did Alexander keep Hephaestion's memory alive in the army?
options: He renamed a city after him only
He forbade anyone to mention him
He appointed no replacement and kept the cavalry unit under Hephaestion's name
quiz.explanation: He left the command unfilled so the unit would still be called Hephaestion's.

cards.title: The end can come mid-plan, so say what matters now
cards.body:
In June 323 BC, in Babylon in what is now Iraq, Alexander fell ill after days of feasting and drinking. The Royal Diary, which Arrian follows, shows him carried to the daily sacrifices and still giving orders for an invasion of Arabia, even as the fever worsened. Then he lost his voice. His soldiers forced their way in to see him. Unable to speak, he greeted each of them with his right hand, lifting his head with difficulty and signalling with his eyes.

He died at 32, after a reign of twelve years and eight months. Some said that when asked who should rule after him, he answered, 'To the best.' Plans can wait forever; goodbyes cannot.
cards.quote: yet he greeted each of them with his right hand, raising his head with difficulty and making a sign with his eyes.
cards.locator: Chapter XXVI. Alexander’s Death ¶1
cards.apply_it: Is there someone you keep meaning to thank or reconnect with? Do it this week, before the next plan.

quiz.question: According to some authors, what did Alexander answer when asked to whom he left his kingdom?
quiz.explanation: Some writers say he replied 'To the best', leaving his generals to fight over the empire.

cards.title: Know your one craving, because it will drive everything
cards.body:
Closing his history, Arrian sums up Alexander's character. He was handsome, tireless, quick-minded and brave, eager for danger and devoted to the gods. He saw what needed doing before anyone else, could read where events were heading, and was a master at arming, organising and inspiring an army. He kept his agreements, was hard to trick, spent little on himself and lavishly on his friends.

One line stands out: of the body's pleasures he had perfect control, but of the mind's, praise was the one he could never get enough of. That single hunger runs through the whole book, from the Granicus to Gedrosia. Most of us have one craving like that. Knowing it helps us steer it.
cards.quote: In regard to the pleasures of the body, he had perfect self-control; and of those of the mind, praise was the only one of which he was insatiable.
cards.locator: Chapter XXVIII. Character of Alexander ¶1
cards.apply_it: Name the one thing you crave that most shapes your choices. How might it be steering you right now?

quiz.question: What does Arrian say was the one pleasure Alexander could never get enough of?
quiz.explanation: Arrian says Alexander controlled bodily pleasures, but praise was the one pleasure of the mind he could not satisfy.

cards.title: The cure for a wrong is to admit it openly
cards.body:
Arrian does not hide Alexander's faults: hot temper, anger, and a growing taste for the style of Persian kings. He explains them partly by youth, an unbroken run of success, and courtiers who urged him toward the worst. But he praises one thing above all: Alexander, he says, was the only ancient king who repented of his mistakes.

Most people, Arrian observes, try to hide a wrong by defending it as right. The better way is to confess it and be seen to regret it. That eases the hurt for those who were wronged, and gives the wrongdoer real hope of not repeating it. It is as true of a friend, a parent or a boss as of a king.
cards.quote: But it seems to me that the only cure for sin is for the sinner to confess it, and to be visibly repentant in regard to it.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIX. Apology for Alexander’s Errors ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of one mistake you've defended rather than owned. Apologise for it plainly, without excuses.

quiz.question: Why does Arrian say open repentance helps those who were wronged?
options: It lets them forget it happened
Their suffering seems less intolerable when the wrongdoer admits fault
quiz.explanation: Arrian says the hurt becomes easier to bear when the person responsible confesses they acted badly.

cards.title: Before you condemn someone, look at the whole of them, and yourself
cards.body:
Arrian ends with a challenge to anyone quick to call Alexander a bad man. First, he says, gather all his deeds into view, not only the faults. Then consider who you are yourself, and how small your own efforts often are by comparison. Arrian has criticised Alexander throughout, for the killing of Clitus, the burning of Persepolis, the cruelty to Bessus. He says he did so for truth's sake and to help readers. Yet he is not ashamed to admire him.

It is a model for judging anyone, especially in history: name the wrongs clearly, including the immense human cost of conquest, but look at the whole person before passing a final verdict.
cards.quote: Whoever therefore reproaches Alexander as a bad man, let him do so; but let him first not only bring before his mind all his actions deserving reproach, but also gather into one view all his deeds of every kind.
cards.locator: Chapter XXX. Eulogy of Alexander ¶1
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you've written off. List three things they've done well alongside your complaint.

quiz.question: Why does Arrian say he recorded Alexander's bad actions?
options: For the sake of truth and the benefit of readers
To make him look worse than other kings
quiz.explanation: He says he branded those actions as bad out of regard for truth and for the benefit of mankind.
